summaryEn: Taiwan's largest maker of the brown corrugated board that everything ships in — made mostly from recycled waste paper. Operating profit hit a ten-year low, then recovered 22%; one recent quarter earned three quarters of the previous full year. The shares still trade below book value.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; containerboard framing — the FY2025 operating profit recovery of 21.88% from a ten-year low, four-year-high operating margin and the genuine 2026Q1 acceleration credited (with net margin close to operating margin confirming no large one-off), but the collapse from NT$2.27 (FY2022) to NT$0.55 (FY2024) with loss quarters, the dividend cut from NT$1.9 to NT$0.45, and a 4.37% ROE behind the sub-book valuation stated plainly; sector 造紙工業 → Containerboard & Packaging)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Cheng Loong (正隆, TWSE: 1904) makes the **brown corrugated board and boxes that almost everything is shipped in**. Founded in **1959** and **listed in September 1971**, it is Taiwan's largest producer of **industrial paper** — containerboard, corrugated packaging and paper containers — manufactured overwhelmingly from **recycled waste paper**, with operations in Taiwan, mainland China and **Vietnam**.

It is an unglamorous business with a useful characteristic: **demand is derived from the movement of goods**. Every carton of electronics, every case of fruit, every e-commerce parcel needs board. That makes Cheng Loong a proxy for industrial and retail activity — and, because containerboard is a commodity made from a commodity input, it makes profitability a function of **the spread between recovered paper prices and board prices, minus a very large energy bill**.

That spread went badly wrong. Annual EPS collapsed from **NT$2.27 (FY2022) to NT$0.83 (FY2023) to NT$0.55 (FY2024)**, with **loss-making quarters in 2023Q2 and 2025Q2**, and **operating profit fell to a ten-year low**. The dividend followed it down: from **NT$1.9 (FY2021) to NT$1.1, NT$0.5, and NT$0.45**, where it has stayed for two years. The shares fell below book value and remain there at **0.80× book**.

**FY2025 was the turn.** Revenue fell **4.85% to NT$42.98bn**, but **operating profit rose 21.88% to NT$1.88bn**, recovering from that ten-year low; net profit rose **36.01% to NT$823m** and EPS reached **NT$0.74**. Gross margin came in at **17.98%** and operating margin at **4.38%** — the latter a **four-year high**.

**And the most recent quarter was dramatically better still.** **2026Q1 delivered EPS of NT$0.56 — about three-quarters of the entire preceding financial year — in three months**, against **NT$0.08** a year earlier. Gross margin reached **20.6%** and operating margin **6.7%**, both well above the full-year FY2025 figures. Importantly, **the net margin of 6.0% sat close to the operating margin of 6.7%**, which means this was **genuine operating improvement rather than a one-off gain** — a distinction that several other companies in this collection fail.

The balance sheet is that of a heavy-industry paper maker: **NT$73.0bn of assets on NT$30.5bn of equity, a 58.3% debt ratio and NT$6.32bn of cash**, with **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$1.16bn** comfortably above **NT$624m of net profit**. Trailing **return on equity is still only 4.37%**, which is why a company now earning at an improved rate trades at **0.80× book and 2.11% yield**.

The honest read: **a capital-heavy commodity packaging business emerging from its worst period in a decade, with one very strong quarter that is real and not yet a trend — priced below the accounting value of its own assets.**

Cheng Loong was founded in **1959**, as Taiwan's manufacturing economy began to take shape. Every economy that makes and moves physical goods needs **industrial paper**: the brown corrugated board that becomes shipping cartons. It is not a product anyone thinks about, and it is required in enormous quantity by everyone who ships anything. The company **listed in 1971**.

The business is built on **recycling**. Containerboard is made predominantly from **recovered waste paper** — old cartons collected, pulped and re-formed into new board. That makes Cheng Loong one of Taiwan's largest recyclers by volume as a matter of ordinary operation rather than environmental positioning, and it means the company's principal raw material is a **traded commodity** whose price moves with collection volumes, Chinese import policy and global demand.

The economics that follow are stark and worth stating plainly. A paper mill is an **enormous fixed asset that consumes enormous amounts of energy** — pulping and drying paper is one of the most energy-intensive industrial processes there is. Revenue is the **price of board multiplied by tonnes sold**. Cost is **recovered paper plus energy plus depreciation**, most of which does not vary with output. So **profit is a thin spread on a very large revenue base**, and small movements in waste paper prices, board prices or energy costs produce large movements in earnings.

That is exactly what the last several years demonstrated. Board prices weakened, energy costs rose, and Chinese overcapacity pressed on regional pricing. **Operating profit fell to a ten-year low**, EPS collapsed from **NT$2.27 to NT$0.55**, two quarters recorded outright losses, and the dividend was cut by more than three-quarters.

Cheng Loong's response has been geographic and operational: expanding in **Vietnam**, where manufacturing relocation is creating new packaging demand, maintaining its Chinese operations, and working the cost base. **FY2025's 21.88% recovery in operating profit** and the sharp improvement in **2026Q1** are the first evidence that it is working.

- **1959 (4 Feb)** — Cheng Loong founded to make industrial paper for Taiwan's developing manufacturing economy.
- **1971 (10 Sept)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1904)**.
- **1970s–2010s** — Becomes Taiwan's largest containerboard and corrugated packaging producer, built on **recycled waste paper**, and expands into mainland China and **Vietnam**.
- **2020–2021** — Strong years: dividends of **NT$1.8** and **NT$1.9**.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$2.27**; dividend falls to **NT$1.1** as conditions weaken.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$0.83**, including a **loss in Q2**; dividend cut to **NT$0.5**.
- **2024** — **The trough: FY2024 EPS NT$0.55**; gross margin down to **15.9%**, operating margin **3.8%**; **operating profit reaches a ten-year low**; dividend **NT$0.45**.
- **2025** — **The turn.** Revenue falls **4.85% to NT$42.98bn**, but **operating profit rises 21.88% to NT$1.88bn**, net profit **+36.01% to NT$823m**, **EPS NT$0.74**. Gross margin **17.98%**, operating margin **4.38%** — a **four-year high**. Q2 still records a small loss; Q4 earns **NT$0.57**. Dividend held at **NT$0.45**.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$0.56**, roughly three-quarters of all of FY2025 in one quarter, against **NT$0.08** a year earlier. Gross margin **20.6%**, operating margin **6.7%**, net margin **6.0%**. Operating cash flow **NT$1.16bn** against **NT$624m** of net profit.
- **2026 outlook** — Management describes itself as **cautiously optimistic**, citing warming demand on both sides of the Taiwan Strait and continued growth in **Vietnam**.

Cheng Loong's accounts describe **a commodity manufacturer emerging from its worst stretch in a decade**.

- **The collapse, then the turn.** Annual EPS: **NT$2.27 (FY2022) → 0.83 (FY2023) → 0.55 (FY2024) → NT$0.74 (FY2025)**, with **loss-making quarters in 2023Q2 and 2025Q2**. **FY2024 operating profit reached a ten-year low.** FY2025 then delivered **operating profit up 21.88% to NT$1.88bn** and **net profit up 36.01% to NT$823m** — on revenue that **fell 4.85% to NT$42.98bn**. Margin recovery, not volume growth.
- **Margins at a four-year high, and improving further.** FY2025 gross margin **17.98%** and operating margin **4.38%** — the latter the best in four years. Quarterly progression: gross margin **15.9% (2024Q4) → 21.0% (2025Q4) → 20.6% (2026Q1)**; operating margin **3.8% → 7.1% → 6.7%**.
- **The most recent quarter is genuinely strong, and genuinely operational.** **2026Q1 EPS of NT$0.56** was about **three-quarters of the whole of FY2025** in a single quarter, against **NT$0.08** a year earlier. Critically, the **net margin of 6.0% sat close to the operating margin of 6.7%** — meaning **no large non-operating item flattered the result**. This is real operating improvement, and it distinguishes Cheng Loong from several companies in this collection whose headline quarters did not survive that test.
- **Cash flow confirms it.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$1.16bn** against **NT$624m of net income** — the roughly 1.9× ratio a heavily depreciated paper mill should produce.
- **A heavy balance sheet.** **NT$73.0bn of assets** on **NT$30.5bn of equity** — a **58.3% debt ratio** — with **NT$6.32bn of cash**. Paper mills are enormous fixed assets, and this leverage is the reason earnings swing so far in both directions.
- **The dividend records the downturn.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.8 (2020) → NT$1.9 (2021) → 1.1 (2022) → 0.5 (2023) → 0.45 (2024) → NT$0.45 (2025)** — a **76% cut** from the peak, held flat for two years. The **2.11% yield** at NT$21.35 is modest.
- **Trailing return on equity is 4.37%**, and the shares trade at **0.80× book** — the market valuing the company **below the accounting worth of its assets**, which is the standard treatment for a capital-heavy commodity producer earning less than its cost of capital.

The financing reality: **a large, leveraged, energy-intensive asset base that stopped earning properly for three years and has just started again — with the improvement visible in operating margin and confirmed by cash.**

**Stance: Taiwan's largest containerboard maker recovering from a ten-year low in operating profit, with a genuinely operational quarter behind it — earning 4.37% on equity and trading at 0.80x book.**

The bull case:

1. **The recovery is real and testable.** FY2025 **operating profit rose 21.88%** from a ten-year low, operating margin reached a **four-year high of 4.38%**, and **2026Q1 delivered EPS of NT$0.56 — about three-quarters of the entire prior year** — with **net margin (6.0%) close to operating margin (6.7%)**, confirming it was operations rather than a one-off.
2. **Cash flow supports it.** **NT$1.16bn of operating cash flow against NT$624m of net income** in 2026Q1.
3. **Priced below its own assets.** **0.80× book** for Taiwan's largest producer in its category. If earnings normalise toward historical levels, both the earnings and the multiple would re-rate.
4. **Structural demand and geography.** Containerboard demand tracks goods movement, which is stable over time; and **Vietnam** is growing as manufacturing relocates there — a genuine expansion market, with management citing warming cross-strait demand as well.

The counter-arguments:

- **The earnings history is poor.** **NT$2.27 → 0.83 → 0.55**, with **outright loss quarters in 2023Q2 and 2025Q2**. One good quarter does not undo three bad years.
- **Return on equity is 4.37%** — well below any reasonable cost of capital, which is precisely why the shares sit below book.
- **The dividend was cut 76%** and has been flat at **NT$0.45** for two years; the **2.11% yield** offers little while waiting.
- **Leverage and energy intensity.** A **58.3% debt ratio** on assets that consume enormous energy. Both amplify any renewed weakness.
- **The spread is not controlled by the company.** Recovered paper prices, board prices and energy costs are all external, and Chinese overcapacity continues to press regional pricing.

A **deep-value cyclical** thesis: real, cash-confirmed improvement at a sub-book price — where the question is whether one quarter becomes a trend.

Cheng Loong converts **used cardboard into new cardboard**, at industrial scale:

- **The raw material.** **Recovered waste paper** — collected old cartons — is the principal input, supplemented by virgin pulp. This makes the company one of Taiwan's largest recyclers by volume as a matter of ordinary operation, and it means the **key input is a traded commodity** whose price moves with collection rates, import policy and regional demand.
- **The process, and why energy dominates.** Waste paper is pulped, cleaned, formed and **dried** into containerboard. Drying paper requires enormous quantities of heat, making paper mills among the **most energy-intensive industrial operations** in any economy. Energy is therefore one of the largest cost lines, and its price is another thing the company does not control.
- **The products.** **Containerboard** (the base material), **corrugated board and boxes** (converted packaging sold to manufacturers, food producers and e-commerce operations), and **paper containers**. Demand is derived from **the movement of goods** — anything shipped needs a box.
- **The geography.** Taiwan, mainland China and **Vietnam**, the last growing as manufacturing relocates there and generates local packaging demand — the same relocation visible in Johnson Health Tech's Vietnamese plants and SCSB's Vietnamese branches elsewhere in this collection.
- **Why the margin is thin and volatile.** Revenue is **board price × tonnes**. Cost is **waste paper + energy + depreciation**, and the last two barely vary with output. So the operating margin is a **thin spread on a large revenue base** — **4.38% for FY2025, a four-year high** — and modest moves in any of the three inputs swing earnings dramatically. That is why **FY2022's NT$2.27 became FY2024's NT$0.55**, and why **2026Q1's operating margin of 6.7% produced three-quarters of a full year's earnings in three months**.

The levers are **containerboard prices, recovered paper costs, energy costs, capacity utilisation and the Vietnamese expansion**. The strength is scale in an essential, stable-demand product with a recycling-based supply chain. The vulnerability is that **it is a leveraged, energy-hungry commodity business where the entire profit is a spread between prices set elsewhere.**

Containerboard is one of the world's most fundamental industries and one of its most persistently low-return ones.

- **Why it exists and does not go away.** Every physical good that moves does so in packaging, and corrugated board is the default. Demand tracks **industrial production and retail volumes**, including e-commerce, and is therefore stable over long periods — but it is also **entirely derived**, with no ability to create its own demand.
- **Why returns are structurally poor.** Paper machines are **enormous, long-lived, capital-intensive assets** that must run continuously to be economic. When demand softens, producers keep producing and prices fall — the same dynamic seen in flat glass at **Taiwan Glass (1802)** elsewhere in this collection. Add **energy intensity** and a commodity raw material, and the result is a thin, volatile spread.
- **The Chinese factor.** Chinese containerboard capacity is vast, and its import policy on recovered paper has repeatedly reshaped global waste-paper flows and prices. Regional producers, including Taiwanese ones, take the consequences on both the input and output side.
- **The Taiwanese landscape.** Cheng Loong is the largest domestic industrial paper producer, competing with **Yuen Foong Yu (1907)** — also in this collection, though weighted more toward cultural paper and diversified materials — and other regional mills.
- **Where growth actually is.** Not Taiwan, where volumes are mature, but **Vietnam and Southeast Asia**, where manufacturing relocation is creating new packaging demand from a low base. Management has specifically cited continued Vietnamese growth alongside warming cross-strait demand.
- **The recycling angle is economics, not marketing.** Containerboard has been made from recovered fibre for decades because it is cheaper, not because it is virtuous. That does, however, position the industry favourably as packaging regulation tightens around recyclability and recycled content.

Cheng Loong's position is **the strongest available in a structurally difficult industry**. The industry truth is that **containerboard producers earn their money in the years when the spread is wide and give it back in the years when it is not** — and that the sub-book valuations attached to them reflect a genuine, persistent gap between returns and the cost of the capital employed.

**Strengths**
- **Taiwan's largest containerboard and corrugated packaging producer**, working from recycled waste paper, with operations in Taiwan, mainland China and **Vietnam**.
- **FY2025 recovery**: operating profit **+21.88% to NT$1.88bn** from a ten-year low; operating margin **4.38%**, a four-year high.
- **2026Q1 genuinely operational**: EPS **NT$0.56** (about three-quarters of all FY2025), with **net margin 6.0% close to operating margin 6.7%** and **operating cash flow 1.9× net income**.
- **Priced at 0.80× book** — below the accounting value of the assets.

**Weaknesses**
- **Three poor years**: EPS **NT$2.27 → 0.83 → 0.55**, with loss quarters in **2023Q2 and 2025Q2**.
- **Trailing ROE 4.37%** — below any reasonable cost of capital.
- **Dividend cut 76%** from NT$1.9 to NT$0.45, flat for two years; **2.11% yield**.
- **58.3% debt ratio** on an extremely energy-intensive asset base.

**Opportunities**
- **Vietnam growth** as manufacturing relocates; warming cross-strait demand.
- Continued margin recovery toward historical levels; e-commerce packaging volumes.
- Tightening packaging regulation favouring recycled-content producers.

**Threats**
- **Energy cost increases** in one of the most energy-intensive industries.
- **Chinese overcapacity** pressing regional board prices.
- Recovered paper price volatility compressing the spread from the input side.

- **The profit is a thin spread between prices set elsewhere (the structural risk).** Revenue is board price times tonnage; costs are recovered paper, energy and depreciation. **Operating margin was 4.38% for FY2025 — a four-year high.** At that level, modest adverse moves in any of the three inputs eliminate the profit, which is exactly what produced **loss-making quarters in 2023Q2 and 2025Q2**.
- **One quarter is not a recovery.** **2026Q1's NT$0.56** was excellent and — importantly — **operational**, with net margin close to operating margin. But it follows **three years of EPS at NT$2.27, 0.83 and 0.55**, and the company's **trailing return on equity is still 4.37%**.
- **Energy intensity.** Drying paper is among the most energy-hungry industrial processes. Electricity and fuel price increases flow almost directly into the cost base, and Taiwan's electricity pricing is itself subject to policy decisions.
- **Chinese overcapacity.** Vast Chinese containerboard capacity and shifting Chinese recovered-paper import policy affect both the price Cheng Loong pays for input and the price it can charge for output.
- **Leverage.** A **58.3% debt ratio** on **NT$73.0bn of assets** against **NT$30.5bn of equity**. Fixed financing costs against a thin, volatile operating margin is what turns a soft year into a loss-making quarter.
- **Little income while waiting.** The dividend has been **NT$0.45 for two years** after a **76% cut**, giving a **2.11% yield**. An investor in this recovery is paid almost entirely in the hope of it happening.

Cheng Loong's outlook depends on **whether one strong quarter becomes a year.** The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin.** The single number that matters. It ran **3.8% (2024Q4) → 4.38% (FY2025, a four-year high) → 6.7% (2026Q1)**. Holding near 6–7% for a full year would represent a genuine change in the company's earning power; slipping back to 4% would mean 2026Q1 was a favourable moment in the spread.
- **Full-year EPS against the history.** **NT$2.27 (FY2022) → 0.55 (FY2024) → 0.74 (FY2025)**, with **NT$0.56 in 2026Q1 alone**. If the run rate holds even approximately, FY2026 would be the best year since 2022 — and a company at **0.80× book with a 4.37% ROE** would look very different.
- **Input costs.** Recovered paper and energy prices set the spread. Neither is forecastable, but both are observable, and both determine whether the margin holds.
- **Vietnam and cross-strait demand.** Management's stated grounds for cautious optimism. Vietnamese growth is the only structural volume expansion available; Taiwanese volumes are mature.
- **The dividend.** Held at **NT$0.45** for two years after a **76% cut**. An increase would be management's own confirmation that the recovery is durable.

Bottom line: Cheng Loong makes **the corrugated board that everything ships in**, from **recycled waste paper**, at scale across Taiwan, China and Vietnam — a business that fell to a **ten-year low in operating profit**, cut its dividend **76%**, and traded down to **0.80× book**. It has now posted **FY2025 operating profit up 21.88%**, a **four-year-high operating margin**, and a **2026Q1 that earned about three-quarters of the entire prior year with net margin close to operating margin and cash flow to match** — genuine improvement, not an accounting artefact. Judge it on **operating margin sustained over a full year** — a cheap, leveraged commodity asset that has just started working again.
